name: Oriya (Odia)
variety: Standard Odia (educated speech of Cuttack, Puri and Bhubaneswar)
sources: Ray, Tapas S. (2003). Oriya. In Cardona, George & Jain, Dhanesh (eds.), The Indo-Aryan Languages. London: Routledge.
Neukom, Lukas & Patnaik, Manideepa (2003). A Grammar of Oriya. Arbeiten des Seminars für Allgemeine Sprachwissenschaft 17. Zürich: Universität Zürich.
Masica, Colin P. (1991). The Indo-Aryan Languages. Cambridge University Press.

Khan, Sameer ud Dowla (2016). The intonation of South Asian languages: towards a comparative analysis. Proceedings of Formal Approaches to South Asian Languages 6, 23-36 (areal intonation pattern only).
contrasts: four-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates: voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced, breathy voiced
dental versus retroflex stops; /n/ : /ɳ/; /l/ : /ɭ/ (retroflex lateral, kept in Odia unlike Bengali and Hindi)
six vowel qualities /i e a ɔ o u/ with no length contrast: the long and short i and u of the script sound alike
a single sibilant /s/ for the three letters ଶ ଷ ସ; [ʃ] only in some clusters
every consonant letter without a vowel sign is followed by /ɔ/, also at the end of a word: there is no schwa deletion (ଘର /ɡʱɔɾɔ/ 'house')
allophony: /ɖ ɖʱ/ are flaps [ɽ ɽʱ] between vowels, written ଡ଼ ଢ଼
[ɛ] occurs as a variant of /e/ and from the fusion of /j/ with a following /a/ or /ɔ/
ଯ is /dʒ/, ୟ is /j/; ଜ୍ଞ is [ɡj] with a nasalised vowel, କ୍ଷ is [kʰj]
syllable_structure: (C)(C)V(C); most native words end in a vowel; clusters occur mainly in Sanskrit loans
phonotactics: word-final consonants are rare in native words because the inherent vowel is pronounced
/ɳ ɭ ŋ/ do not occur word-initially
geminates are distinguished by some speakers, mostly in Sanskrit loans

stress.rule: No agreed rule: stress is not prominent in Odia and is one of the least studied parts of its phonology.
stress.cues: unknown; probably the pitch of the phrasal rise

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none: all vowels, including final /ɔ/, are fully pronounced
rhythm.notes: Class and final lengthening are assumptions from the areal pattern; no measurement could be verified.

length.notes: No vowel length contrast. Geminates are marginal; no duration figures could be verified.

intonation.declarative: presumably the areal pattern: a rise on each content word phrase, low at its start and high at its end, and a final fall to low
intonation.wh_question: prominence on the wh-word, final fall
intonation.continuation: high right edge on non-final phrases
intonation.notes: No instrumental description of Odia intonation is known to me; the entries follow the pattern shared by the South Asian languages that have been studied (Khan 2016).

phonation: breathy voiced stops and affricates /bʱ d̪ʱ ɖʱ dʒʱ ɡʱ/

problems: ଘ is a plain [ɡ] at the start of a word and after a vowel (the first rule for the letter gives g, not g#): ଘର comes out as [ɡɔɾɔ].
ଳ is the syllabic l phoneme of the base table followed by a long vowel: ଫଳ [pʰɔl̩ɔː], ଜଳ [ɟɔl̩ɔː], କମଳ [kɔmɔl̩ɔː] gain a syllable, and there is no retroflex lateral.
ଣ is always [n] (ପାଣି [pani], ମଣିଷ [mɔnisɔ]); the retroflex nasal is lost.
One phoneme /dʒ/ has two sounds: ଜ is the palatal stop phoneme [ɟ], ଯ is [dʒ].
ଜ୍ଞ is [ɡɡ] (ଜ୍ଞାନ [ɡɡanɔ]) and କ୍ଷ is doubled [kʰkʰ] (ଲକ୍ଷ୍ମୀ [lɔkʰkʰmi]).
The translator uses the Hindi settings (stress on the last heavy syllable) with the Bengali phoneme table.
Breathy voiced stops come from the Hindi base table (voiced closure plus voiceless aspiration sample); /ɦ/ is voiceless [h]; intonation uses the generic tunes.
good: the final inherent vowel is kept (ଭାରତ [bʰaɾɔtɔ], ରାମ [ɾamɔ])
the three sibilant letters are all [s]

notes: The standard references describe the sound system without instrumental data; I could not verify any formant, VOT or duration figures for Odia, so those fields are left out. Nasal vowels are listed for all six qualities; their functional load is low.
